case_study_insert.main_stem: Wayline Driving School (WDS) is a private limited company in the education and training sector, operating eight franchised driving schools and employing a workforce of 24. Founded in 2011 by Tomas Byrne, the business operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. WDS plans to invest $300,000 in eight dual-control vehicles and a digital booking platform for three new franchise locations, financed by a $180,000 hire purchase agreement and $120,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $128,000 a year, a variable cost of $22.00 a unit and a selling price of $38.00, and currently produces 13,500 units a year, measured in one-to-one lessons. WDS faces rising lesson-cancellation rates and a shortage of certified instructors.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2026: The eight schools delivered 3,240 lessons last quarter with an average cancellation rate of 14%, up from 11% a year ago. First-time pass rate is 61%. Complaints about instructor punctuality fell from 17 to 9 per month. Average booking-to-lesson wait is 6 days. A survey of 400 learners found that 71% want more evening and weekend slots and 58% would pay up to $4 more for a guaranteed weekly slot. Five of 24 instructors have not completed refresher training; off-the-job training at the regional training centre costs $450 per employee. WDS is also trialling hybrid dual-control cars at two schools.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Wayline Driving School for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, the third rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for variable-rate and hire purchase agreements. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $12.30 to $13.10 per hour from April 2026, raising wage costs for instructors and office staff. (3) Unleaded petrol prices have risen 13.5% year-on-year and motor insurance premiums for dual-control cars are up 15.2%, while consumer spending on driving lessons grew 2.8% in the same period.

questions.question_text: WDS plans to finance part of its fleet expansion with hire purchase. Explain two advantages for WDS of using hire purchase to fund the eight dual-control vehicles instead of a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the cost of the eight dual-control vehicles over their working lives, matching monthly instalments to the lesson revenue the fleet generates. WDS keeps its cash for fuel, insurance and the new booking platform rather than paying out $180,000 upfront, which protects working capital while fixed costs already stand at $128,000 a year.

Point 2: The vehicles themselves act as security for the hire purchase agreement, so WDS avoids pledging all its business assets as collateral, unlike a bank loan secured across the whole company. Ownership transfers automatically once the final instalment is paid, the agreement is straightforward to arrange at the point of vehicle purchase, and there is no large balloon repayment — suiting a private limited company funding a $300,000 expansion with $120,000 retained profit and limited spare cash.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Wayline Driving School and its fleet expansion decision.

questions.question_text: WDS is launching its winter intensive-course promotion. Consider national television advertising, local newspaper advertising, or door-to-door flyer drops across nearby estates. Which should WDS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: Television would put the winter intensive course in front of millions and build instant brand recognition across all eight franchise catchments. However, production and airtime costs are prohibitive for a 24-employee business funding a $300,000 expansion largely through hire purchase, and most national viewers live outside the school's teaching areas, so the spend-to-enrolment ratio would be very poor for a local service.

Local newspaper advertising: Regional papers are read by parents of prospective learners in exactly the neighbourhoods WDS serves, carry strong local trust, and cost a fraction of television. They suit timed offers such as the winter promotion and can be repeated weekly through January. The limitation is modest reach — circulation is declining and younger learners increasingly discover services online rather than in print.

Door-to-door flyer drops: Flyers are extremely cheap per household, hyper-local around each of the eight schools, and ideal for households with 17-year-olds. However, they are easy to ignore, unmeasurable, create litter and waste, and cannot carry the detailed course information learners want — and much of each estate includes households with no learner driver.

Recommendation: WDS should choose local newspaper advertising. It balances reach and cost across all eight catchments, carries trust with parents of young learners, and supports the timed winter offer better than scattergun television or easily-binned flyers. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a regional driving school; door-to-door flyers are rejected as too narrow, wasteful and unmeasurable, though a small flyer run around the three new locations could reinforce the newspaper campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of WDS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of WDS with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and flyers are rejected.

questions.question_text: WDS's flat structure and autocratic leadership shape how its front-line instructors work. Explain two benefits for WDS of using autocratic leadership when managing its driving instructors.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership gives WDS's 24 instructors clear, non-negotiable standards — for safety, vehicle checks, punctuality and pupil conduct — which is essential when mistakes can kill. Decisive direction from Tomas Byrne's management team means every school applies the same rules, the 61% first-time pass rate stays consistent across franchises, and complaint counts like the punctuality complaints that fell from 17 to 9 per month keep falling.

Point 2: Autocratic leadership enables fast decisions when operational problems hit: for example, re-allocating instructors immediately when cancellations (now averaging 14%) spike, authorising cover for sickness or pushing a winter promotion live within days. In a flat structure with a wide span of control there is little middle-management friction, so urgent calls are made without committee delays — protecting the 13,500 lessons delivered a year and the digital booking platform's promise of 6-day booking turnaround.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WDS's safety needs, cancellations and franchise consistency.

questions.question_text: WDS faces a shortage of certified instructors for its three new franchise locations. Consider recruiting experienced instructors externally or retraining existing part-time instructors internally. Which should WDS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
External recruitment: Bringing in experienced, certified instructors fills the gap immediately, unlocks the three new locations on schedule, brings fresh teaching techniques and competitor insight, and keeps the digital booking platform's 6-day promise intact. The drawbacks are salaries above current averages, advertising and interview costs, a 6-week-plus notice period for many employed candidates, and cultural risk as newcomers learn WDS's safety-first standards from scratch.

Internal retraining: Retraining existing part-time instructors is far cheaper — 5 staff through off-the-job training at $450 each is just $2,250 — retains loyalty, rewards ambition, and produces instructors who already know WDS's routes and pupils. However, it reduces teaching capacity while staff train, cannot run faster than the certification process, and leaves the three new sites under-staffed during the launch window, with 71% of learners demanding more evening slots.

Decision: WDS should recruit experienced instructors externally for the three new locations, while continuing internal retraining as a second wave. The launch window is fixed and external hires protect revenue from 13,500 potential extra lessons; internal-only is rejected because it cannot staff three new sites fast enough to meet the 71% demand for evening and weekend slots. Off-the-job training remains essential — external hires should complete the $450 refresher within their first month to standardise safety practices.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two recruitment options with limited application to WDS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both options in the context of WDS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of WDS with a well-justified decision covering speed, cost and launch timing.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how WDS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $128,000 ÷ ($38.00 − $22.00) = $128,000 ÷ $16.00 = 8,000 lessons. Answer: break-even output is 8,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $38.00 − $22.00 = $16.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $16.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways WDS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 8,000-unit break-even with 13,500 lessons delivered shows a margin of safety of 5,500 units (about 41% of output), signalling that the fleet expansion is affordable and that demand can slip meaningfully before WDS makes losses.
2. Contribution data lets WDS price the winter intensive course: the 58% premium slot idea worth $4 a lesson would lift contribution to $20.00, so managers can forecast exact profit impact before committing marketing spend.
3. Unit cost data — ($128,000 ÷ 13,500) + $22.00 = $31.48 per lesson — lets managers benchmark instructor productivity, spot vehicles or routes wasting fuel, and renegotiate supplier pricing as petrol inflation reaches 13.5%.
4. Labour productivity of 13,500 ÷ 24 = about 563 lessons per instructor lets managers set realistic instructor workloads for the three new franchises, identify underused staff and justify external recruitment where gaps appear.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 8,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $16.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 5,500 units versus 13,500 lessons produced; premium pricing modelling for the $4 guaranteed slot requested by 58% of learners; unit-cost benchmarking at $31.48 to counter 13.5% petrol inflation; and productivity targets of about 563 lessons per instructor to staff the three new locations.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate WDS's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has WDS's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 36.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 18.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit $414,000 on revenue of $1,150,000 (414 ÷ 1,150 = 36.0%); 2025 gross profit $552,000 on revenue of $1,380,000 (552 ÷ 1,380 = 40.0%). Operating profit rose from $138,000 (138 ÷ 1,150 = 12.0% of revenue) to $207,000 (207 ÷ 1,380 = 15.0% of revenue). With capital employed of $920,000 in 2024 and $1,150,000 in 2025, the return on capital moved from 138 ÷ 920 = 15.0% to 207 ÷ 1,150 = 18.0%. Revenue grew $230,000 (20.0%) while cost of sales grew only $92,000 (12.5%), reflecting the 58% appetite for guaranteed slots and steady lesson-pricing power.

Evaluation: Performance has improved across all three measures. Even though cancellations worsened from 11% to 14%, the 58% appetite for guaranteed slots at $4 extra lifted average revenue per lesson, and interest payable rose only from $18,000 to $26,000 ahead of the fleet expansion. Risks remain: petrol costs are up 13.5%, motor insurance premiums for dual-control cars are up 15.2%, the 6.5% minimum wage rise arrives in April 2026, and 71% of learners want more evening slots, straining instructor capacity.

Conclusion: WDS's financial performance has improved — profitability (36.0% to 40.0%), operating margin (12.0% to 15.0%) and return on capital employed (15.0% to 18.0%). The trend is genuine but fragile; WDS must protect it by cutting cancellations below 11%, locking in fuel purchasing, and using the new booking platform to fill evening capacity before wage and insurance inflation bite.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs and capital movements and a justified conclusion on whether WDS's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: WDS is trialling hybrid dual-control cars at two of its schools. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WDS of switching its fleet to hybrid dual-control vehicles.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Hybrid dual-control cars use far less petrol per mile, which directly counters the 13.5% year-on-year fuel inflation and protects the $22.00 variable cost per lesson. They also appeal to environmentally aware learners and parents, strengthening WDS's local reputation at a time when consumer spending on driving lessons grew only 2.8%, and helping the brand stand out among eight competing franchises across the city.

Disadvantage: Hybrids cost more to buy than conventional dual-control cars, increasing the upfront strain on the $300,000 expansion and pushing up hire purchase instalments at a time when motor insurance premiums are already up 15.2%. Their specialist servicing also requires training and parts that may not be stocked locally, risking longer off-road downtime — a serious problem when the fleet must deliver 13,500 lessons a year and three new locations are already understaffed.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WDS's fuel costs, fleet expansion and launch capacity.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 13.5% rise in fuel costs will affect WDS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): WDS's $180,000 hire purchase would cost roughly 0.75% more a year — about $1,350 extra — and any variable-rate borrowing or overdraft would rise similarly. Higher rates also squeeze household budgets, potentially delaying enquiries for driving lessons, though consumer spending on lessons still grew 2.8%. The direct cash impact is small and the rate can be negotiated or the term restructured.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $13.10): Instructors deliver about 13,500 one-hour lessons a year. The 6.5% rise adds about $0.80 per lesson-hour on the pre-rise rate of $12.30, or roughly $10,800 a year across 13,500 lesson-hours, plus knock-on pay pressure for office staff. This lands just as WDS adds three new franchise locations and needs more headcount, and it cannot be passed fully into the $38.00 lesson price without risking enrolment.

Fuel cost inflation (13.5%): Teaching cars cover an estimated 240,000 miles a year across eight schools. If fuel spend is about $50,000 a year, a 13.5% rise adds roughly $6,750 annually, and insurance premiums for dual-control cars are separately up 15.2%. Fuel cannot be avoided in a driving school, but efficient route planning and the hybrid trial mitigate it over time.

Conclusion: The 6.5% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It adds roughly $10,800 a year against about $6,750 of fuel inflation and $1,350 of extra hire purchase interest, hits on every one of 13,500 lesson-hours, and strains the marginal economics of the three new franchises. WDS must renegotiate hire purchase terms and instructor rotas, pass modest price rises into the $4 premium slot offer, and accelerate the fuel-efficient hybrid rollout to protect the 15.0% operating margin.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to WDS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on WDS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of WDS with a well-justified judgment that the minimum wage rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
